extra.message: Flask Debug Mode Enabled (Active Debug Code)

metadata.proof: SOURCE: `debug=True` is hardcoded in `app.run()` at line 24. SINK: This enables the Werkzeug interactive debugger. Any unhandled exception reveals detailed stack traces with source code snippets. extra.message: No rate limiting on authentication endpoint enabling brute-force

metadata.proof: SOURCE: unlimited HTTP POST requests from an attacker. SINK: the sqlivuln handler (line 9) executes the vulnerable SQL authentication query on every invocation with zero throttling, delay, or account-lockout mechanism. An attacker can send thousands of requests per second to brute-force credentials or repeatedly exploit the SQL injection (already found at line 16) without any request cap, exponentially increasing the probability of successful compromise.

extra.message: Request headers (potentially containing auth tokens) printed to stdout

metadata.proof: SOURCE: the incoming HTTP request's Headers object (request.headers) which may contain Authorization, Cookie, X-API-Key, Set-Cookie, or other sensitive tokens. SINK: stdout (console/log output). When an attacker or any user sends a request, all header key-value pairs are unconditionally printed to the application's stdout. In containerized or production deployments, these logs are collected, stored, and often accessible to monitoring/ops personnel who may not be authorized to see authentication secrets.

extra.message: No authentication or authorization on any API endpoint

metadata.proof: SOURCE: the OpenAPI specification (lines 10-100) defines ten API paths (/xssnovuln, /xssreflected, /lfinovuln, /lfivuln, /rfinovuln, /rfivuln, /hhinovuln, /hhivuln, /sstinovuln, /sstivuln, /sqlinovuln, /sqlivuln) with zero security requirements or securitySchemes defined anywhere in the file. SINK: all handler functions are invocable by any unauthenticated caller. An attacker can freely invoke file-read (LFI), network-request (SSRF), template-injection (SSTI), database-query (SQLI), and header-injection (HHI) endpoints without providing any credential, API key, or session token.

extra.message: Outdated dependency pins swagger-ui version with known XSS vulnerabilities

This version bundles an outdated swagger-ui (3.x) known to contain reflected XSS and open-redirect vulnerabilities (e.g., CVE-2021-46708). SINK: the application serves swagger-ui at /ui/ at runtime. extra.message: Plaintext Password Storage — Passwords stored as raw VARCHAR with no hashing

metadata.citation: table ="""CREATE TABLE USERS(USERNAME VARCHAR(255), PASSWORD VARCHAR(255));"""
metadata.proof: The USERS table schema at custom_db.py:16 defines PASSWORD as a plain VARCHAR column. Lines 27 and 30 then INSERT raw passwords ('kaines', 'admin') without any hashing (no bcrypt, PBKDF2, SHA-256, or even a salted hash). The sqli.py:20 response returns the full row including the plaintext password in the API response. Anyone who compromises the database file or exploits the SQL injection gets usable cleartext passwords.

extra.message: Missing CSRF Protection — Login endpoint accepts POST with no anti-CSRF token

metadata.proof: The /sqlivuln POST route (swagger.yml:151, handler sqli.py:9) performs authentication without any CSRF protection. No CSRF token is required, validated, or even generated. There is no Flask-WTF, no @csrf.exempt decorator, and no CSRF middleware registered in app.py. The Connexion/Flask application does not enable CSRF protection anywhere. An attacker can craft a cross-origin form that silently submits credentials and logs the victim into the attacker's account, or triggers unintended state-changing actions on behalf of an authenticated user.

extra.message: Binding to All Network Interfaces — Server listens on 0.0.0.0

metadata.proof: The Flask/Connexion development server at app.py:24 binds to 0.0.0.0, exposing the application on all available network interfaces. Combined with debug=True (already reported as CWE-489), this makes the Werkzeug debugger console accessible from any machine that can reach the host's IP address on port 8000. An attacker on the same network or with network access can trigger exceptions and interact with the interactive debugger to execute arbitrary Python code.

extra.message: User / Account Enumeration via Login Response Differential

metadata.citation:
cur.execute(f"SELECT * FROM USERS WHERE USERNAME='{username}'")
users = cur.fetchall()
...
return {"msg": f"Hello, {users}"}, 200
metadata.proof: SOURCE: untrusted 'username' obtained from request body via sqli.get('username', 'noprovided') at line 10. PROCESSING: the string-interpolated SQL query at line 16 fetches users matching only the username (password never validated), and fetchall() at line 17 returns either a populated list or empty list. SINK: line 20 serialises the list into the response — existing usernames produce {"msg": "Hello, [('admin', 'admin')]"} while non-existing usernames produce {"msg": "Hello, []"}. Additionally, line 19 returns raw SQL error text when an exception occurs. An attacker can script requests across candidate usernames and distinguish the three response shapes to build a list of valid accounts, which then enables targeted brute-force or credential-stuffing attacks.

extra.message: Denial of Service via Unbounded File Read — open().read() buffers entire file into memory

metadata.proof: Attacker sends POST /api/lfivuln with {"filename": "/dev/zero"} or a large log file. lfi.py:13 extracts the attacker-controlled filename from the request body, passes it to fetchfile() at lfi.py:16, which calls open(name).read() at line 3 with NO size limit. The entire file contents are read into a single Python string in memory. Special device files like /dev/zero produce infinite output, exhausting all available RAM and crashing the process. No file-size check, no chunked read, no timeout.

extra.message: Denial of Service via Unbounded HTTP Response Body — requests.get().text buffers entire response into memory

metadata.proof: Attacker POSTs /api/rfivuln with {"imagelink": "https://attacker.com/large"} pointing to a server that streams data at high speed. rfi.py:15 extracts the attacker-controlled URL from the request body, passed to fetchimage() at rfi.py:18. At line 5, requests.get() is called with stream=False (default), so .text downloads and decodes the ENTIRE response body into memory before returning. The 2-second timeout only caps the download window — a server on a fast link can deliver hundreds of MB within that window. Multiple concurrent requests multiply the effect, exhausting process memory.
